I wanted to build a file-sharing website.

Naturally, that turned into a deep dive into cloud storage, database architecture, and IP-based rate limiting. 😂

Here's what's powering FileGuard:

☁️ Backblaze B2 for file storage
🗄️ Neon PostgreSQL for metadata
🐍 Python + Flask for the backend
📦 Dynamic ZIP creation for entire folders
🛡️ Subnet-based quotas to help limit abuse

And yes, files are designed to expire after 12 hours.

No accounts. No unnecessary friction. Just share, download, and move on.

Tomorrow: The actual launch. 🚀

#CloudComputing #BackendDevelopment #BuildInPublic

I tried to destroy my own app. 💀

So, I built a Bit-Flip Attack Simulator for FileGuard. I wanted to see how the system behaves if someone attacked it. Best way to do thatw as to attack it myself.

The idea is simple:
🧪 Modify a file stored in the system.
🔍 Run a SHA-256 integrity check.
🚫 Block the download if the file's contents no longer match the original.

Basically, if someone messes with the file, FileGuard shouldn't just shrug and send it anyway.

Because “it downloaded successfully” doesn't necessarily mean “it's the right file.”

Next up: The infrastructure behind it. ☁️

DOWNLOAD SPEED = 600 Mbps. 🚀👀

And apparently, you don't necessarily need a faster internet plan to get there.

I just discovered Plexo, an open-source download manager that combines multiple independent internet connections to speed up downloads.

📶 Wi-Fi + Jio + Airtel  
⚡ Multiple connections. One download.  
💻 Available for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

The idea is ridiculously cool: Plexo splits downloads into chunks, pulls them across multiple networks, and reassembles the file.

Of course, your actual speed depends on your connections and the download server. But seeing this technology in action is seriously impressive.

Free. Open source. No ads.

This is the kind of project that makes me love discovering cool tech.
